question: Which cells in the pancreas produce insulin?
explanation: Beta cells located within the islets of Langerhans are responsible for synthesizing and secreting insulin. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: What is the primary role of the exocrine pancreas during digestion?

options.A: Secreting digestive enzymes into the duodenum
options.B: Producing glucagon to maintain glucose levels
options.C: Storing bile produced by the liver
options.D: Releasing insulin directly into the bloodstream

explanation: The exocrine tissue uses acinar cells to manufacture and release enzymes that break down food components in the small intestine. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h1)

question: The main mechanism of tissue damage in acute pancreatitis is...

options.A: excessive production of red blood cells
options.B: complete destruction of islet beta cells
options.C: bacterial invasion from the large intestine

explanation: Proteolytic enzymes activate inside the pancreas rather than the duodenum, causing auto-digestion of the gland. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: Gallstones cause acute pancreatitis by doing what to the duct system?

options.B: Destroying the sphincter of Oddi completely
options.C: Dilating the main pancreatic duct permanently
options.D: Blocking the outflow of pancreatic secretions

explanation: An obstructing gallstone prevents digestive juices from reaching the small intestine, increasing intraductal pressure and triggering inflammation. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h2)

question: A hallmark clinical sign of chronic pancreatitis resulting from fat malabsorption is...
explanation: Steatorrhea involves bulky, pale, foul-smelling stools caused by the body's inability to digest and absorb dietary fats. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: A patient with acute pancreatitis complains of severe pain. Where does this pain typically radiate?
explanation: Inflammation of the retroperitoneal pancreas commonly produces a penetrating abdominal pain that radiates straight through to the back. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which blood test is more specific for diagnosing acute pancreatitis than amylase?
explanation: Lipase is considered more specific to the pancreas because it stays elevated longer and originates almost exclusively from pancreatic tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: Why is an abdominal ultrasound commonly ordered early in acute pancreatitis?

options.A: To assess long-term endocrine function of the organ
options.B: To measure exact blood glucose and insulin levels
options.C: To check for gallstones blocking the biliary tract
options.D: To remove necrotic tissue from the pancreatic duct

explanation: Ultrasound is a non-invasive imaging method excellent for identifying biliary stones as the precipitating trigger for the attack. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h4)

question: The primary goal of keeping a patient with acute pancreatitis NPO is to...

options.A: prevent the sudden development of severe hyperglycemia
options.B: eliminate the need for intravenous fluid administration
options.C: allow the kidneys to recover from contrast dye injury
options.D: reduce pancreatic stimulation and enzyme secretion

explanation: Withholding oral food and fluids prevents the gastrointestinal tract from releasing hormones that stimulate pancreatic enzyme production. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: A patient with severe acute pancreatitis is at high risk for which electrolyte imbalance?
explanation: Fat necrosis releases free fatty acids that bind with calcium in the abdominal cavity, dropping serum calcium levels significantly. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h5)

question: The most common type of malignant tumor found in the pancreas is...
explanation: Ductal adenocarcinoma accounts for the vast majority of all pancreatic malignancies. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: A tumor located in the head of the pancreas frequently causes which clinical finding?
explanation: Obstruction of the common bile duct by a head-of-pancreas tumor causes conjugated bilirubin to back up into the bloodstream and tissues. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h6)

question: Another name for the pancreaticoduodenectomy surgery is the...
explanation: A pancreaticoduodenectomy is widely referred to in clinical practice as the Whipple procedure. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: Which structures are typically removed during a standard Whipple procedure?

options.A: Head of the pancreas, duodenum, gallbladder, and part of the bile duct
options.B: Body and tail of the pancreas along with the entire stomach
options.C: Gallbladder, spleen, and lower portion of the esophagus
options.D: Entire pancreas, spleen, left kidney, and descending colon

explanation: The procedure resects the pancreatic head, adjacent duodenum, distal common bile duct, and gallbladder due to their shared blood supply and proximity. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h7)

question: What is the most critical and feared complication following a Whipple procedure?
explanation: Leakage of enzyme-rich fluid from the surgical reconnection site can cause severe intra-abdominal infection and vessel erosion. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)

question: A nurse caring for a patient post-pancreatectomy should prioritize monitoring which parameter closely?
explanation: Removing part or all of the pancreas disrupts insulin-producing tissue, putting the patient at risk for unstable blood sugar levels. [learn more](GNS222_U2_T7#GNS222_U2_T7_h8)
